opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think vibe coding is one of the most interesting things happening right now, and I'd split it into two pieces.

The first is what most people picture: someone who maybe isn't a professional engineer describes what they want, the model writes the code, and they never really read it. They just check whether it works. For prototypes, internal tools, a weekend project, or a quick way to show a designer what you mean, that's fantastic. It lowers the cost of trying an idea to almost nothing, and a lot of software that never would have existed now gets written.

Professional software development is a different problem. Writing the first version was never really the hard part. The hard part is maintaining it, making sure it's secure, getting it to work with a huge existing codebase, and having someone who understands why it does what it does when it breaks at 2 a.m. Vibe coding in the pure sense, where you don't look at the code, doesn't solve any of that. If anything, it can create a pile of code that nobody understands.

So I think in professional settings it turns into something more like delegation. The engineer acts more like a tech lead. You break the problem down, hand pieces to the model, review what comes back, and decide what's good enough. The skill moves from typing code to specifying clearly and reviewing well. Those were always the skills that set senior engineers apart, and now they matter for everyone.

The thing I'd watch is verification. As models get better at longer, more autonomous tasks, the bottleneck becomes how fast a human can confirm the output is correct. Teams that invest in good tests, good evals, and clean architecture will get much more out of these tools than teams that just turn on the firehose. Vibe coding ends up rewarding software engineering discipline rather than replacing it.

r001.rationale: The response praises vibe-coded prototypes but does not predict that professional engineers will replace them.

r002.rationale: It says vibe coding can leave “a pile of code that nobody understands,” presenting that as a problem for professional maintenance.

r003.rationale: It does not say that rewriting an unfamiliar codebase is often cheaper than maintaining it.

r004.rationale: The response calls for engineers to review work and understand why code behaves as it does, but does not clearly state that humans need to retain a high-level understanding of the codebase.

r005.rationale: It recommends breaking problems into pieces for the model, but does not connect that approach to projects exceeding the AI’s ability to understand them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think vibe coding is real, and I think it matters, but it's important to be precise about what it is and what it isn't.

The way I'd describe it: vibe coding is when you stop reading the code. You describe what you want, the model writes it, you run it, and if it doesn't work you just tell the model what went wrong and let it try again. You're steering by the behavior of the program, not by the text of the program. And for a lot of things that's genuinely fine. If I want a little script to reformat a spreadsheet, or a throwaway prototype to see whether an idea feels right, I don't care what the code looks like. The code is disposable. The only thing that matters is whether it does the thing.

Where I think people get confused is when they extrapolate from that to professional software. In a real codebase, the code isn't disposable. It's going to be there for years, other people are going to read it, it's going to be modified a hundred times, and the cost of a subtle bug can be enormous. So the question for a professional engineer isn't really "should I vibe code or not." It's "how much of my attention does this particular piece of code deserve?" And the honest answer is that it varies a lot, even inside a single project.

I think what's actually happening is a shift in where the engineer's judgment gets applied. Historically a lot of your judgment went into writing the code line by line. Increasingly, it goes into specifying the problem well, deciding what the architecture should be, deciding what to test, and deciding which parts you need to read carefully and which parts you can trust. That last skill is new, and I think it's going to become one of the core skills of the job. Knowing when to look closely and when not to.

The other thing I'd say is that the models are getting good enough that the line is moving. Two years ago, vibe coding anything beyond a toy was risky because the model would quietly do something dumb. Now the models are much better at the boring, well-specified parts of software, and a lot of professional software is boring and well-specified. So the territory where you can safely not read the code keeps expanding. But it's not going to cover everything, and I'd be nervous about any team that treats it like it does.

So my view is: vibe coding is a mode, not an identity. Good engineers will drop into it constantly for the parts of the work where it's appropriate, and they'll drop out of it for the parts where it isn't. The people who struggle will be the ones who can only do one or the other.

r002.rationale: It says professional code must be maintainable and read by others, but does not characterize a codebase its maintainers do not understand as a net liability.

r004.rationale: It mentions making architectural decisions and choosing what to read carefully, but does not clearly state that humans need to retain a high-level understanding of the codebase.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a spectrum. If you’re building a prototype, you can describe what you want, see what the model produces, and iterate very quickly. You may care much more about whether the experience works than about how the code is organized. That’s a useful way to explore an idea.

In professional software development, though, getting something working is only part of the job. You also have to understand how it fits into the system, how you’ll test it, and how someone will maintain it six months later. Vibe coding doesn’t remove those responsibilities.

So I think it fits as a way to get to a first version faster, and increasingly as a way to implement well-defined pieces of a larger system. The engineer still needs to decide what to build and what evidence is sufficient to trust it. As generating code gets cheaper, that judgment becomes a bigger part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response says vibe coding can speed up a first version, but does not predict that PM prototypes will be replaced by software rebuilt by professional engineers.

r002.rationale: It discusses understanding a system as a professional responsibility, but does not characterize an unfamiliar codebase as a net liability.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim that rewriting an unfamiliar codebase from scratch is often cheaper than maintaining it.

r004.rationale: It says engineers should understand how code fits into the system, but does not clearly state that humans need to retain a high-level understanding of the codebase.

r005.rationale: It does not describe decomposing projects into AI-manageable subproblems as a way to handle projects beyond the AI’s understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it fits at different points depending on what you’re trying to build. If you’re exploring an idea, being able to describe what you want and get something working quickly is incredibly useful. You can try things you wouldn’t have bothered to build before because the cost was too high.

In professional software development, though, getting something working is only part of the job. You need to know whether it’s correct, whether it’s secure, and whether someone can maintain it six months from now. So you can move very quickly while you’re exploring, but as that code becomes something people depend on, you need review, testing, and an understanding of what the system is doing.

I think the interesting shift is that writing the code becomes less of the bottleneck. Figuring out what to build, specifying the behavior, and deciding whether the result is good become a much larger part of the engineer’s work.
